title_en: MacroVoices #554 Yasir Arafat: Mass Manufacturing Nuclear Power Plants
title_zh: MacroVoices #554 Yasir Arafat（Aloe Atomics）：量产核电站
subtitle_zh: Aloe Atomics CTO 谈如何像造汽车一样量产核电站，让核能便宜过煤电和气电。
description: MacroVoices #554 Yasir Arafat: Mass Manufacturing Nuclear Power Plants

turns.en: But it's not a matter of whether or not we want to transition to nuclear. It's a matter of when, because if you compare those same numbers with oil and gas, oil and gas will only last us 50 more years worldwide to run civilization.
turns.zh: 但这不是我们要不要转向核能的问题，而是什么时候转的问题。因为如果拿同样的数字去跟石油和天然气比，全球化石燃料只够维持人类文明再运行50年。

turns.en: That was Aloe Atomic's co-founder and CTO, Yasser Arafat. I'm Eric Townsend, and this is Macrovoices, the free weekly podcast targeting professional finance and sophisticated private investors.
turns.zh: 刚才那段是 Aloe Atomics 联合创始人兼 CTO Yasir Arafat。我是 Eric Townsend，这里是 MacroVoices，一档面向专业金融人士和成熟个人投资者的免费周播节目。

turns.en: Episode 554 was produced on October 15, 2026. This week, I'm pleased to introduce you to Yasser Arafat, co-founder and chief technology officer of Aloe Atomics.
turns.zh: 第554期节目制作于2026年10月15日。本周，我很高兴向大家介绍 Aloe Atomics 的联合创始人兼首席技术官 Yasir Arafat。

turns.en: You heard Yasser's partner and Aloe CEO, Matt Lozak, introduce Aloe's plan to mass-produce not just nuclear reactors, but entire nuclear power plants in Macrovoices Episode 522, which aired on March 5, 2026.
turns.zh: 在2026年3月5日播出的 MacroVoices 第522期节目中，Yasir 的合伙人、Aloe CEO Matt Lozak 已经介绍过 Aloe 的计划——不只是量产核反应堆，而是量产整座核电站。

turns.en: This week, we're going to move beyond Aloe's immediate plans to deliver behind-the-meter nuclear energy for data centers and talk about what it's really going to take.
turns.zh: 本周，我们将超越 Aloe 为数据中心提供表后（behind-the-meter）核能的近期计划，聊聊到底需要什么条件。

turns.en: Not just for Aloe, but for the entire US advanced nuclear industry to scale nuclear energy using advanced technology up while bringing the cost of nuclear energy down to the point that it eventually costs less than coal and gas.
turns.zh: 不只是 Aloe，而是整个美国先进核能行业，如何用先进技术把核能规模化，同时把核能成本降下来，最终降到比煤电和气电还便宜。

turns.en: And I'll tell you up front, Yasser really surprised me in this interview. I thought he was going to say it takes at least 15 years to get to that point where we can make nuclear energy cost less than coal and gas because I say that's where the demand absolutely explodes and we see a change in the course of human history.
turns.zh: 先跟大家说一声，Yasir 在这次访谈中真的让我吃了一惊。我原以为他会说，至少需要15年才能让核能成本低于煤电和气电，因为我认为到那时需求会彻底爆发，人类历史的进程会就此改变。

turns.en: Yasser thinks it comes much earlier than I was thinking. So I think you're really going to enjoy this interview, folks. I let it run a little bit longer than usual, but I think you'll find it's worth it.
turns.zh: Yasir 认为这个时点会比我预想的早得多。所以大家一定会喜欢这次访谈。我让它比平时长了一些，但你们会觉得值得。

turns.en: Now, I'm Patrick Ceresna. Let's dive straight into this interview. In the interest of full disclosure, I want to acknowledge that I am an early investor in Yasser's company, Aloe Atomics.
turns.zh: 好，我是 Patrick Ceresna。让我们直接进入访谈。为了充分披露，我想说明，我是 Yasir 公司 Aloe Atomics 的早期投资人。

turns.en: In fact, it's the biggest private equity position I've ever held. So I clearly have a vested interest in the company's success and I want to be transparent with our listeners about that interest.
turns.zh: 事实上，这是我持有过的最大一笔私募股权头寸。所以我显然在公司的成功上有切身利益，我想对听众透明地披露这一点。

turns.en: Nothing in this interview is investment advice. Yasser, it's great to have you on the program. I'm really looking forward to this one. Our longtime listeners have already heard your partner Matt Lozak explain Aloe's plan to offer behind-the-meter nuclear power for AI data centers.
turns.zh: 本次访谈内容不构成投资建议。Yasir，非常欢迎你来到我们的节目，我非常期待这一期。我们的老听众已经从你的合伙人 Matt Lozak 那里听过 Aloe 为 AI 数据中心提供表后核电的计划。

turns.en: So today, I want to focus on the longer term, what happens next, and how we really scale nuclear energy up to a whole new level. But for anybody who didn't catch that interview with Matt, let's just start with a quick refresher.
turns.zh: 所以今天我想聚焦更长期的话题：接下来会发生什么，我们如何真正把核能提升到一个全新的水平。但对于没听过 Matt 那期访谈的人，我们先来快速回顾一下。

turns.en: What business is Aloe in today and what are your current plans? Thank you, Eric, for having me on and interviewing Matt and also bringing the Aloe story to light and your continued support and supporting Aloe.
turns.zh: Aloe 目前在做什么业务，你们的当前计划是什么？谢谢 Eric 邀请我上节目，也谢谢你采访了 Matt，把 Aloe 的故事带给大家，还有你一直以来的支持。

turns.en: So for those of the audience who are not familiar or need a refresher, Aloe is building mass manufactured nuclear reactors. Now when we do this, our first market we are targeting is AI data centers because they're the ones who need energy most urgently than anyone else.
turns.zh: 对于不熟悉或者需要复习的听众，Aloe 正在建造量产型核反应堆。我们首个目标市场是 AI 数据中心，因为他们是最迫切需要能源的群体。

turns.en: Once we deploy there and essentially come down the cost curve, that unlocks other markets for us. It's very similar to how Bezos, when he started Amazon, he started with books initially.
turns.zh: 一旦我们在那里部署并沿成本曲线下来，就会为我们打开其他市场。这非常像 Bezos 当年创办 Amazon 时，一开始做的是图书。

turns.en: And then later, he came up with the everything store. So just like books for Amazon, data centers are sort of our books. We start up with data centers, but then when we come down the cost curve, every other country who is importing energy to keep their lights on, our communities who are struggling with energy, all of that opens up for us.
turns.zh: 后来他才提出了“万物商店”（everything store）的概念。所以就像图书之于 Amazon，数据中心就是我们的图书。我们从数据中心起步，但当我们沿成本曲线下来后，所有靠进口能源维持供电的国家、所有为能源发愁的社区，都会向我们敞开。

turns.en: Thanks, Yasser. Listeners in case you missed it, I strongly recommend listening to Aloe CEO Matt Lozak's interview back on Macrovoices Episode 522, which aired on March 5th, 2026.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Yasir。听众朋友们，如果你们错过了，我强烈建议去听 Aloe CEO Matt Lozak 在2026年3月5日播出的 MacroVoices 第522期访谈。

turns.en: Yasser, the nuclear industry has been around for 75 years and we still have less than 450 power reactors operating worldwide. That's about six units a year of established long run demand.
turns.zh: Yasir，核能行业已经发展了75年，但全球运行的动力反应堆还不到450座。按长期既定需求算，也就是每年大约6座。

turns.en: And frankly, that's hardly enough to justify any kind of grown up conversation about mass producing anything. Yet, you're already building a factory right now in Texas to mass produce 100 nuclear reactors per year on an assembly line.
turns.zh: 坦率地说，这几乎不足以支撑任何关于量产的严肃讨论。可你们现在已经在 Texas 建厂，要在流水线上量产每年100座核反应堆。

turns.en: Now, this is not my personal view, but I know a lot of investors are going to be very skeptical and maybe even think you're crazy because they're going to say, look, there's obviously not enough volume to justify assembly line production of nuclear reactors, which historically take a decade to build and cost tens of billions of dollars per project.
turns.zh: 这不是我个人的观点，但我知道很多投资人会非常怀疑，甚至觉得你疯了。他们会说：“看，显然没有足够的体量来支撑核反应堆的流水线生产，历史上这些项目要建十年，每个耗资数百亿美元。”

turns.en: So how would you answer investors' objections if they think you've frankly lost your mind proposing to mass produce something that the whole industry only built 450 of in 75 years?
turns.zh: 所以，如果投资人认为你提议量产一个整个行业75年只造了450座的东西是彻底疯了，你会怎么回应他们的质疑？

turns.en: It is crazy until somebody proves that it is not. So think about when Elon first coined, he wanted to go build rockets, everyone laughed at him.
turns.zh: 在有人证明它不疯之前，它就是疯的。想想 Elon 最初说要去造火箭的时候，所有人都嘲笑他。

turns.en: And they laughed again when he said he wants to land them and reuse the boosters. And so now every other rocket company is essentially copying off of his model, including China.
turns.zh: 当他说要把火箭降落回收、重复使用助推器时，人们又嘲笑了一次。可现在其他所有火箭公司基本都在照搬他的模式，包括中国。

turns.en: And the other thing to remember is we are not mass producing our grandfather reactors, right? These are not this giant mega scale project that we have seen with massive cooling towers.
turns.zh: 另外要记住的是，我们量产的不是我们父辈那种反应堆。这些不是我们见过的那种带巨大冷却塔的超大规模项目。

turns.en: I mean, this country spent like what, the last 70 years trying to make nuclear cheap by building one really perfect reactor each time it gets bigger every single time we build it until it became so big that no one can really predict how long it'll take or how much it'll cost.
turns.zh: 我是说，这个国家过去70年一直在试图让核能变便宜，方法是每次都造一座真正完美的反应堆，而且每造一次就更大一次，直到大到没人能真正预测要多久、要花多少钱。

turns.en: But if you think about Vogle, which is the first nuclear plant the country has built after 35 years of not building anything, it took twice as long and more than twice the budget, right?
turns.zh: 但如果你想想 Vogtle——这是美国在35年没建任何核电站之后建的第一座——它花了两倍的时间，预算也超了一倍多，对吧？

turns.en: So what we're talking about here in Analo is really trying to reinvent how we go about nuclear. You don't make nuclear cheap by building one perfect reactor and hope that it works out.
turns.zh: 所以我们在 Aloe 这里真正要做的，是重新发明搞核能的方式。你不是靠造一座完美的反应堆然后祈祷它成功来让核能变便宜的。

turns.en: You make it cheap by building the same good reactor a thousand times and improving it at every generation. So when we picked out our design, we didn't think about, okay, what is the nicest thing that can work on paper?
turns.zh: 你是靠把同一款好反应堆造一千遍，每一代都改进它，才让它便宜。所以当我们选定设计时，我们想的不是“纸面上最漂亮的东西是什么”。

turns.en: We said we picked out our design that can produce the most power you can put on the back of a truck. So we have to design that once and build many.
turns.zh: 我们说，我们要选那种能装在一辆卡车后斗上的、功率最大的设计。所以我们只需要设计一次，然后造很多座。

turns.en: Right? That's our starting point. If you go to any race, you have to pick out the best horse. And the best horse that we picked was sodium cold reactor technology.
turns.zh: 对吧？这就是我们的起点。就像你去参加任何赛马，你得挑最好的那匹马。我们挑中的最好的马是钠冷反应堆技术。

turns.en: This can give us the highest density reactor technology and still get to market in the near term. But what's interesting, Eric, is that, you know, yes, we are going from a 40,000 square feet facility to a million square feet and scale up our production to 100 reactors.
turns.zh: 它能给我们最高密度的反应堆技术，同时还能在近期上市。但有意思的是，Eric，你知道，是的，我们要从4万平方英尺的厂房扩到100万平方英尺，把产能提升到100座反应堆。

turns.en: It's so interesting to see like how the market is so real because when we talk to customers, they're calling us up and saying, hey, although I don't want one reactor or five reactors or 10, they're asking us literally like, hey, I want to reserve 20% of your factory production capacity.
turns.zh: 看到市场如此真实真的很有意思。因为我们跟客户聊的时候，他们打电话过来说：“嘿，我不要1座、5座或10座反应堆”——他们直接说：“嘿，我想预定你们工厂20%的产能。”

turns.en: And that's kind of an interesting model. We haven't thought about that first. If other three other customers say I want the next 20% and the next 20% and get up to all the way to 80%, that should give us a signal to go build the second factory.
turns.zh: 这是一种很有意思的模式，我们一开始都没想到。如果另外三个客户说“我要下一个20%”、“再下一个20%”，一直凑到80%，那就给了我们一个信号去建第二座工厂。

turns.en: Right? Okay, we can keep supply and demand in these two closely tight steps. You don't want to take supply too far out in the demand. You don't want to have a massive demand and not be able to supply it.
turns.zh: 对吧？好，我们可以让供需保持紧密同步。你不想让供给跑得太超前于需求，也不想有大量需求却供不上。

turns.en: This is one way how to keep those two things in synchronous way. Well, Yasser, I've done a bunch of my own analysis of this and I'm very much with you.
turns.zh: 这是让两者保持同步的一种方式。嗯，Yasir，我自己做过一堆分析，我完全站你这边。

turns.en: I wanted to start with that objection that I know a lot of other investors would have because that's where I started when somebody first said to me, mass producing nuclear reactors on an assembly line.
turns.zh: 我想先谈那个我知道很多其他投资人也会有的质疑，因为当有人第一次跟我说“要在流水线上量产核反应堆”时，我就是这么反应的。

turns.en: I'm like, what are you crazy? There's only 450 of them. When you look at the demand and you look at the desire of energy transition away from fossil fuels that's shared by almost every government on earth, it's a whole other story.
turns.zh: 我会说：“你疯了吗？全世界总共才450座。”但当你看到需求，看到几乎地球上每个政府都有的、想要摆脱化石燃料的能源转型愿望时，那就是另一个故事了。

turns.en: And I'm going to come back to that longer term story later in this interview, but I want to start with how you justify your current plans for AI data centers because that question is what's going to be on the mind of investors who haven't yet done the arithmetic on what the demand could eventually look like.
turns.zh: 我稍后会在访谈里回到这个更长期的故事，但我想先从你如何论证当前面向 AI 数据中心的计划开始，因为这个问题正是那些还没算过需求最终会有多大的投资人心里的疑问。

turns.en: Now I have done that arithmetic and I think there's already considerably more demand just from the AI data centers alone over the next few years.
turns.zh: 我自己已经算过这笔账，我认为未来几年光是 AI 数据中心就已经有相当大的需求。

turns.en: So I predict that the one gigawatt per year, that's 100 of your modular nuclear reactors that you're going to build in the factory that you have under construction right now in Texas, some critics think that's overkill.
turns.zh: 所以我预测，每年1吉瓦——也就是你们在 Texas 正在建的工厂要造的100座模块化核反应堆——有些评论人士认为这过头了。

turns.en: I think it's going to be woefully insufficient. And I would actually go, you know, if you want to know my idea on a business plan, yeah, having some investors come in and say, well, I want to reserve 20%, well, hopefully they're going to give you a bunch of capital in exchange for that contract and help you build the next factory.
turns.zh: 我认为这远远不够。而且我甚至会说，如果你想知道我的商业计划想法，嗯，让一些投资人进来说“我想预定20%”，希望他们会为了那份合同给你一大笔资本，帮你建下一座工厂。

turns.en: But what I'd say is sell 50% of your capacity and then auction the rest of them as they become available and say who wants it fastest and who wants to pay up.
turns.zh: 但我会说，卖掉50%的产能，然后把剩下的拍卖，谁最快要、谁愿意加价就给谁。

turns.en: Anyway, that's a little bit of a tangent. So let me come back to what we wanted to talk about. We'll get back to the crazy stuff later on in the interview.
turns.zh: 好了，这有点跑题了。让我回到我们想聊的话题，疯狂的部分我们稍后再谈。

turns.en: What you're building right now is going to make 100 reactors a year. They're 10 megawatts electric each. That's one gigawatt per year. Some people think that's too much or it's crazy.
turns.zh: 你们现在在建的工厂每年会造100座反应堆，每座10兆瓦电力，也就是每年1吉瓦。有些人觉得这太多了或者疯了。

turns.en: The way that's going to work is these reactors basically come together in what you call pods. A pod is a pre-manufactured nuclear power plant.
turns.zh: 运作方式是这样的：这些反应堆基本上组合成你们所说的 pod（模块）。一个 pod 就是一座预制的核电站。

turns.en: It has five reactors and three steam turbines so that you can run at full nameplate capacity even after one of those steam turbines trips offline.
turns.zh: 它有5座反应堆和3台蒸汽轮机，这样即使其中一台蒸汽轮机跳闸下线，你也能以全额铭牌容量运行。

turns.en: So it's redundant, it's designed for data centers, it's modular, it's built in a factory and your factory is going to build 20 of those pods.
turns.zh: 所以它有冗余，是为数据中心设计的，是模块化的，是在工厂里造的，而你们的工厂每年会造20个这样的 pod。

turns.en: Each pod has five reactors so that's your 100 reactors. How big, I think it's actually bigger than you think frankly but I want to get your numbers.
turns.zh: 每个 pod 有5座反应堆，所以就是100座反应堆。多大？我觉得实际上比你想的要大，坦率讲，但我想听你的数字。

turns.en: How much demand do you think there is in the behind the meter data center market over the next five to 10 years? Is this one factory going to service at all?
turns.zh: 你认为未来5到10年，表后数据中心市场的需求有多大？这一座工厂能全部满足吗？

turns.en: Is it more than that and if so how much more than that and what's the plan for the second or the third factory? Yeah, there's a lot of questions in that one question.
turns.zh: 如果不止，那多多少？第二座、第三座工厂的计划是什么？是啊，这一个问题里有一堆问题。

turns.en: Sorry. And now I'll try to appeal this layer by layer. So first things first, in the near term we're always going to be supply limited. So you're not wrong, your arithmetic is actually on the spot here.
turns.zh: 抱歉。现在我会试着层层拆解。首先，近期我们永远都会是供给受限的。所以你没说错，你的算术非常准。

turns.en: The 100 reactor goal is not the end goal. It is the starting point in our journey for mass production. Our first factory, what we're saying is like, hey, I want to get to from making 1Z2Z reactors to 100 reactors a year and at that time I can really start answering some of the key questions that matter, meaning like is the factory truly scalable, right?
turns.zh: 100座反应堆的目标不是终极目标，而是我们量产之旅的起点。我们的第一座工厂，我们说的是：“嘿，我要从造1座、2座反应堆提升到每年造100座。”到那时我才能真正开始回答一些关键问题，比如工厂是否真的可扩展，对吧？

turns.en: Do I have infrastructure? Do I have the machines? Do I have the people? Do I have the process laid out that can be scalable from there? When I build the supply chain that comes with us, even though we tout as being a vertically integrated nuclear company, which we are, we don't make everything, we still rely on raw materials like steel, sensors, pumps, electronic components, and then we make stuff
turns.zh: 我有基础设施吗？我有机器吗？我有人吗？我有可以从那里扩展的流程吗？当我建立起随我们成长的供应链时——尽管我们标榜自己是一家垂直整合的核能公司，我们确实是——但我们不是什么都造。我们仍然依赖钢材、传感器、泵、电子元件等原材料，然后我们用这些原材料或大宗商品材料造东西，对吧？

turns.en: out of those raw materials or commodity materials, right? Next thing you have to answer yourself is like, okay, if I go to 100 reactors a year, can I fuel these?
turns.zh: 接下来你要回答自己的问题是：好，如果我做到每年100座反应堆，我能给它们供燃料吗？

turns.en: Can I find the supply chain to make sure fuel is available? Not for their initial deployment, but every fuel cycle. I have to go replenish this fuel every three to four years.
turns.zh: 我能找到供应链确保燃料可用吗？不只是初次部署，而是每个燃料循环。我每3到4年就得补充一次燃料。

turns.en: Once these are proven, then we can think about, okay, how do we now scale up from here to meet the demand to truly make a dent? This market is so massive.
turns.zh: 一旦这些得到验证，我们才能想：好，那我们现在如何从这里扩大规模来满足需求，真正做出改变？这个市场太庞大了。

turns.en: I mean, we were talking about data center. Why did we pick data center market? First of all, in the last 70 years, we have not seen a market demand this big, wanting this much amount of power so quickly.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们在谈数据中心。我们为什么选数据中心市场？首先，在过去70年里，我们没见过一个市场需求这么大、这么快就要这么多电力。

turns.en: I mean, just to give you an idea, every organization quotes different numbers, but Bank of America, for example, they said, hey, we need 125 gigawatts, 125 gigawatts, each gigawatt roughly power a million homes, just to give you an idea.
turns.zh: 给你个概念，每家机构引用的数字都不一样，但比如 Bank of America 说：“嘿，我们需要125吉瓦。”125吉瓦，每吉瓦大约能给100万户家庭供电，给你个概念。

turns.en: So over from 2026, from this year to 2030, we need 125 gigawatts. And right now, I believe the grid and everybody else, they can pull together about 25 gigawatt or so.
turns.zh: 所以从今年2026年到2030年，我们需要125吉瓦。而目前，我相信电网和其他所有人加起来只能凑出大约25吉瓦。

turns.en: They've got a 100 gigawatt generation gap on what the demand is. So this market, just the data center alone is massive. And the reason we want to solve the problem there is because we want them to not become a burden to the grid or the communities that rely on that grid.
turns.zh: 他们有100吉瓦的发电缺口相对于需求。所以光是数据中心这个市场就极其庞大。我们想在那里解决问题的原因是，我们不想让它们成为电网或依赖电网的社区的负担。

turns.en: Right? We want to make sure that we provide that electricity, but also provide that reliability of like 99.9% availability or 59 reliability that the only place they can get that reliability is the grid itself.
turns.zh: 对吧？我们想确保我们提供电力，同时也提供那种99.9%可用性或5个9的可靠性——他们唯一能得到这种可靠性的地方就是电网本身。

turns.en: So that's the whole reason why our product from a traditional nuclear speak is so unique. It's very an odd architecture, if you think about it, right?
turns.zh: 所以这就是为什么我们的产品从传统核能角度来说如此独特。如果你想想，这是一种很奇特的架构，对吧？

turns.en: A pod, which is a 50 megawatt device, has five reactors connected to a single steam header with three 25 megawatt turbines, kind of an odd configuration, if you think about it, right, if you look at all the other designs.
turns.zh: 一个 pod 是50兆瓦的装置，有5座反应堆连接到一根蒸汽总管上，配3台25兆瓦的轮机。如果你看看所有其他设计，这是一种挺奇特的配置，对吧？

turns.en: And the reason it's designed that way is because before we started designing on paper, on the technology side, we looked into the market, we talked to a lot of data center companies and we asked them like, hey, what's important to you guys?
turns.zh: 之所以这样设计，是因为在我们开始在纸上做技术设计之前，我们先调研了市场，跟很多数据中心公司聊过，问他们：“嘿，什么对你们最重要？”

turns.en: And over and over again, we heard reliability and it's not just data centers, it's everybody else that wants similar kind of power if they go behind the meter.
turns.zh: 我们一遍又一遍听到的答案是可靠性。而且不只是数据中心，所有想走表后路线的人都想要类似的电力。

turns.en: They want to make sure that close to 100% of the time electricity is available. And that's the reason the pod is designed the way it is. If one of the five reactors is down for refueling or maintenance, the other four can make up its full capacity power for nameplate.
turns.zh: 他们想确保接近100%的时间都有电。这就是 pod 这样设计的原因。如果5座反应堆中有一座因为换料或维护停机，其他4座可以补足它的全部铭牌容量电力。

turns.en: Same on the turbine side, you need only two out of the three turbines to make the full 50 megawatt. If one of them is down for major or minor overhaul or maintenance work, you already have the two running.
turns.zh: 轮机侧也一样，你只需要3台轮机中的2台就能发出全额的50兆瓦。如果其中一台因为大修或小修停机，你已经有2台在运行了。

turns.en: There is something called a product market fit when it comes to nuclear and what kind of market you're going after. And again, I know I'm trying to answer all of your questions one by one.
turns.zh: 在核能领域，有一种叫产品市场契合（product market fit）的东西，关系到你要打什么市场。再说一次，我知道我在试着逐一回答你所有的问题。

turns.en: And the last one that I want to address is, okay, when we solve that first factory, where do we go? So you've got two paths to meet that demand.
turns.zh: 最后一个我想谈的是：好，当我们解决了第一座工厂的问题，我们要往哪走？所以你有两条路来满足那个需求。

turns.en: One path is pretty straightforward is, okay, I know a million square feet, I can make hundred reactors a year. Now let me go and copy paste two more factories and I can scale up the demand that way.
turns.zh: 一条路很直接：好，我知道100万平方英尺、我每年能造100座反应堆。那让我去复制粘贴再建两座工厂，我就能这样扩大供给来满足需求。

turns.en: Obviously, there's going to be some process improvements and you can make potentially larger capacity out of them. And so it's basically arithmetic, right?
turns.zh: 显然会有一些流程改进，你可能能从中做出更大的容量。所以基本上就是算术，对吧？

turns.en: That's one approach. The other approach is trying to innovate and figure out how can we get more energy out of that same form factor? So the sodium cold reactor technology is one of those technologies that can really pave the pathway to a different kind of reactors called fast spectrum reactors that could potentially extract 60 to 100 times more energy than a once through cycle if you couple that with
turns.zh: 这是一种方法。另一种方法是创新，想办法如何从同样的外形尺寸里获取更多能量。所以钠冷反应堆技术就是那种能真正为另一类反应堆——叫快谱反应堆（fast spectrum reactors）——铺平道路的技术之一。如果你把它跟换料结合起来，快谱反应堆可能能从一次通过循环中提取60到100倍的能量。

turns.en: refueling. So those are the kind of things that we're thinking about constantly, how to figure out how to meet this massive demand that we are seeing today.
turns.zh: 所以这些都是我们一直在思考的事情，如何想办法满足我们今天看到的这个巨大需求。

turns.en: We'll definitely come back to the fuel cycle and what it takes to get to fast spectrum and all of that later in this interview. But first, I just want to recap what you said.
turns.zh: 我们稍后一定会在访谈里回到燃料循环、如何走到快谱等等这些话题。但首先，我想复述一下你说的。

turns.en: You're saying that the gap that's already been identified in the next five years is about 125 gigawatts of which so far people have only stepped up to 25.
turns.zh: 你是说，未来5年已经识别出的缺口大约是125吉瓦，而到目前为止人们只凑出了25吉瓦。

turns.en: That means there's 100 gigawatts missing and the factory you're building is only going to supply one gigawatt per year worth of electric generation capacity.
turns.zh: 这意味着还缺100吉瓦，而你们在建的工厂每年只能供应1吉瓦的发电容量。

turns.en: You're only solving 1% of the problem that's already been established by other people objectively analyzing what the world needs. Now as much as that's a compelling argument, I'm going to make a counter argument that that's just barely scratching the tip of the iceberg because I contend there's one very specific thing that this industry needs to accomplish to completely change the demand story.
turns.zh: 你只解决了别人客观分析世界需求后已经确立的问题的1%。尽管这个论证很有说服力，我要提出一个反论：这仅仅是在刮冰山顶端的一点点，因为我认为这个行业需要完成一件非常具体的事情，才能彻底改变需求的故事。

turns.en: That is that as soon as you figure out, don't care who does it or how it happens, but when somebody figures out to make safe, clean nuclear energy cost less than coal and gas and be deployed just as quickly, I contend demand explodes overnight because look, the whole world wants to get off of fossil fuels, solve this whole problem.
turns.zh: 那就是：一旦有人——不管是谁、不管怎么做——想办法让安全、清洁的核能成本低于煤电和气电，并且部署速度一样快，我认为需求会一夜之间爆发。因为看，全世界都想摆脱化石燃料，解决这整个问题。

turns.en: If you could solve it with nuclear, well, okay, it costs twice as much as coal and gas and it takes 10 years to build and it's next to impossible to bring the capital together.
turns.zh: 如果你能用核能解决，那好吧，它成本是煤电和气电的两倍，要建10年，而且几乎不可能把资本凑齐。

turns.en: If you could change that by selling a modular power plant that comes off an assembly line in the factory that costs less than a coal plant and you can't do that for the next few years, I realize, but if you can get to that some point, it becomes what I call the nuclear Henry Ford moment, the moment in history when it becomes possible to break humanity's addiction to fossil fuels and to restore the level of abundance and prosperity that
turns.zh: 如果你能改变这一点，卖一种从工厂流水线下线的模块化电站，成本比煤电厂还低——我知道未来几年你还做不到，但如果某个时点你能做到，那就成了我所说的核能 Henry Ford 时刻：历史上那个可以打破人类对化石燃料的成瘾、恢复我小时候——1960年代末1970年代初——还记得的那种富足和繁荣水平的时刻。

turns.en: I just barely remember from when I was growing up as a kid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Even after adjusting for inflation, crude oil cost more than double what it did back then and at any price above $87 WTI and right now I'm looking at $94 WTI on my live chart, it's more than triple what it cost when I was a kid even after adjusting for inflation and I think that's the reason we have people living in tents and sidewalks on the streets
turns.zh: 即使经过通胀调整，原油价格也比我小时候高出一倍多。任何高于87美元 WTI 的价格——我现在看着实时图表上是94美元 WTI——都比我小时候的价格高出三倍多，即使经过通胀调整。我认为这就是为什么我们的大城市街头有人住在帐篷里、睡在人行道上。

turns.en: of our major cities. It's because of the unaffordable cost of energy. So if you could figure out how to make modular nuclear power plants that are cheaper than coal and gas, I say it changes everything.
turns.zh: 就是因为能源成本负担不起。所以如果你能想办法造出比煤电和气电更便宜的模块化核电站，我说这会改变一切。

turns.en: So forgive me for my long-windedness in this question, but when I put the numbers together and did my own arithmetic, I couldn't believe it, yes sir.
turns.zh: 所以请原谅我在这个问题上啰嗦，但当我把数字凑在一起、自己算了算，我简直不敢相信。

turns.en: You want to build one gigawatt per year in your first factory. If you wanted to replace the energy that we now depend on fossil fuels for, you'd have to run that factory for 9,000 years to build enough reactors to replace what the world gets.
turns.zh: 你想在第一座工厂每年建1吉瓦。如果你想替代我们现在依赖化石燃料的能源，你得让那座工厂运行9000年，才能造出足够的反应堆来替代世界目前从化石燃料获得的能源。

turns.en: I'm not suggesting that one company is going to solve this whole problem, but imagine that you just wanted a 25% market share as you guys are leading the way into this charge.
turns.zh: 我不是说一家公司能解决这整个问题，但想象一下，如果你们带头冲锋，只想拿到25%的市场份额。

turns.en: Okay, that would mean you'd have to produce at least 112 gigawatts electric per year. That's 112 times what this factory that you're building in Texas is intending to produce and that would only give you a 25% market share.
turns.zh: 好，那意味着你每年至少要生产112吉瓦电力。这是你们在 Texas 建的这座工厂打算生产量的112倍，而那还只能给你25%的市场份额。

turns.en: But wait a minute, it's not that easy because Elon Musk has said that engineering the Tesla was the easy part. Mass production, really building something sophisticated modern technology at the pace of automotive assembly was the hard part.
turns.zh: 但等等，没那么容易，因为 Elon Musk 说过，设计 Tesla 是容易的部分，量产——真正以汽车装配的速度建造复杂的现代技术产品——才是难的部分。

turns.en: So my question is, is it possible ever to make nuclear energy with the technologies that you're working with cost less than coal and gas and be deployed just as quickly as a new coal plant can be built?
turns.zh: 所以我的问题是：用你们正在研发的技术，有没有可能让核能成本低于煤电和气电，并且部署速度和建新煤电厂一样快？

turns.en: And if so, I think it changes the course of human history, but that's a really big both engineering and capital formation challenge. So is it possible and what would it take?
turns.zh: 如果可能的话，我认为这会改变人类历史的进程。但这是一个非常巨大的工程和资本形成挑战。所以这可能吗？需要什么条件？

turns.en: So the simple answer is yes, it is possible and here's how we see the path to get into that point. Now, as I mentioned before, we're basically trying to tackle the 100 reactor goal for our first factory, but in no way, shape or fashion, we want to stay there.
turns.zh: 简单回答是：是的，可能。我们这样看到达那个点的路径。正如我之前提到的，我们基本上是在为第一座工厂攻克100座反应堆的目标，但我们绝不想停留在那里。

turns.en: We want to get to a point where we can get 10 gigawatts a year or 20 or 50 gigawatts a year and solve that. How do we truly scale up? Well, let's walk backwards.
turns.zh: 我们想达到每年10吉瓦、20吉瓦或50吉瓦的水平来解决这个问题。我们如何真正扩大规模？好，让我们倒着推。

turns.en: How do we get to a point where we can be economically competitive compared to coal or natural gas? And what would that really take? And I cannot speak for all of nuclear because everyone has slightly different ways of doing things, but for all of the way we see it, our first of a kind deployment, meaning the first reactor we're going to be deploying out there is actually very cost compelling even today before even I go into volume production.
turns.zh: 我们如何达到在经济上能与煤或天然气竞争的水平？那真正需要什么？我不能代表所有核能公司说话，因为每家做事方式略有不同，但就我们看待它的方式而言，我们的首台（first of a kind）部署——也就是我们要部署的第一座反应堆——即使在今天、还没进入量产之前，成本也已经非常有竞争力。

turns.en: My first of a kind will land us in the mid teams cents per kilowatt hour. And that is completely fine because I've got a lot of customers today whose willingness to pay is significantly above that.
turns.zh: 我的首台会落在每千瓦时中等十几美分的水平。这完全没问题，因为我今天有很多客户的支付意愿远高于此。

turns.en: What customers are really hungry for today is not the lowest cost alternative. They're initially competing for speed to power. That's what a lot of these initial customers are looking for.
turns.zh: 客户今天真正渴望的不是最低成本的替代品。他们最初竞争的是通电速度（speed to power）。这就是很多初始客户在找的东西。

turns.en: How quickly can I get power? That's number one. Number two, it has to be extremely reliable. You can't just build a power plant to go 99.9% available, but then it's only available 40% of the time that's not going to work.
turns.zh: 我能多快拿到电？这是第一位的。第二，它必须极其可靠。你不能建一座号称99.9%可用的电厂，结果实际上只有40%的时间可用——那行不通。

turns.en: So initially they're willing to pay whatever to get to the speed of power. And our initial first of a kind does that. We think that by the time we build our 10th reactor, we can get under 10 cents a kilowatt hour.
turns.zh: 所以最初他们愿意付任何价钱来换取通电速度。我们的首台能做到这一点。我们认为等我们造到第10座反应堆时，我们能降到每千瓦时10美分以下。

turns.en: And when we get to the 50-ish per year capacity, then we would already be competitive with coal and natural gas. And that's not going to happen in just factory number three and four.
turns.zh: 当我们达到每年50座左右的产能时，我们就已经能与煤和天然气竞争了。而这不会等到第三、第四座工厂才发生。

turns.en: That's happening within the first couple of years of production from this first factory. So we're not banking on achieving this very low cost of energy way out into the future.
turns.zh: 这会在第一座工厂投产的头几年内发生。所以我们不是把实现这种极低的能源成本押在遥远的未来。

turns.en: We're planning to get there in the next few years. So that is the one thing that is super, super compelling. And by the way, when we get there, that's not game over.
turns.zh: 我们计划在未来几年内就达到。所以这是超级、超级有吸引力的一点。而且顺便说一句，当我们达到那个点时，游戏还没结束。

turns.en: That is the beginning of all the bigger challenges that we'll have to face from there on because Elon is kind of right, right, is getting to a first of a kind complex machine is hard, but mass manufacturing is 10 times harder.
turns.zh: 那只是我们从那以后要面对的所有更大挑战的开始。因为 Elon 说得有点道理，对吧：造出一台首台复杂机器很难，但量产要难10倍。

turns.en: And he may not be wrong about that because I can build a one of a kind machine, no problem. And what we are seeing is like, I have supply chain and manufacturing capability today to build like 20 reactors a year.
turns.zh: 他可能没说错，因为我可以造一台独一无二的机器，没问题。而我们现在看到的是，我今天有供应链和制造能力每年造20座反应堆。

turns.en: That's not an issue. But the moment you start scaling up to 50, 200, or 200, or 300, what you're going to notice is that some things will start breaking in the supply chain, right?
turns.zh: 那不是问题。但一旦你开始扩大到50、100、200或300座，你会注意到供应链上有些东西会开始断裂，对吧？

turns.en: The challenge comes in when you're trying to build the same thing over and over again. It becomes really hard. And as you scale, that problem becomes harder and harder.
turns.zh: 挑战在于当你试图一遍又一遍地造同样的东西时，会变得非常难。而且随着规模扩大，这个问题会越来越难。

turns.en: And until you go solve all of these changes, it's not going to be a scalable solution. So the one industry that we have seen has truly went through all of that jumps and hoops is really the EV industry, the automotive EV industry, which is why a lot of our team members, a lot of our manufacturing engineers come from background like Tesla, who have done volume production, because manufacturing is really not the biggest problem here alone,
turns.zh: 在你解决所有这些变化之前，它不会是一个可扩展的解决方案。所以我们见过的、真正经历了所有这些跳跃和关卡的行业，其实是电动汽车行业，也就是汽车电动车行业。这就是为什么我们团队的很多成员、很多制造工程师来自 Tesla 这样有量产经验的背景，因为制造本身并不是这里最大的问题。

turns.en: the biggest problem here supply chain. Like we have right now about 230 plus vendors that we rely on. And that number, by the way, is growing.
turns.zh: 这里最大的问题是供应链。比如我们现在依赖230多家供应商。而且这个数字还在增长。

turns.en: And these are companies that I talked about earlier that provide steel, pipe sensors, raw materials. The question is like, yeah, we can go and scale up our facility.
turns.zh: 这些就是我之前谈到的提供钢材、管道、传感器、原材料的公司。问题是，是的，我们可以扩大我们的设施。

turns.en: But how do we convince our vendors and suppliers to scale as we scale? How do they grow their business? How do we inspire them to invest in their production capability so they can come along with us?
turns.zh: 但我们如何说服我们的供应商和随我们一起扩大？他们如何发展业务？我们如何激励他们投资他们的生产能力，让他们能跟我们一起走？

turns.en: That to me is the biggest challenge that we'll have to solve from here forward. But I think it is very possible. We're very confident what technology that we picked is going to get us to the point where when we unlock the volume production, costs will come down so low that this technology become almost a no-brainer to go after.
turns.zh: 对我来说，这是我们今后必须解决的最大挑战。但我认为这非常可能。我们对我们选择的技术非常有信心，一旦我们解锁量产，成本会降得非常低，这种技术几乎会成为不用想就要去采用的选择。

turns.en: At that point, gas turbines will truly become obsolete when it comes to initially data centers and to other markets. Well, Yasser, if you can pull that off in the next few years and get to the point where you're delivering these things at a lower cost than coal and gas and a shorter delivery window in order to get it up into production than coal and gas, I say that changes the course of human history if you can scale it up.
turns.zh: 到那时，燃气轮机在数据中心市场以及其他市场真的会过时。嗯，Yasir，如果你能在未来几年做到这一点，达到以低于煤电和气电的成本交付这些东西、并且比煤电和气电更短的交付窗口投入生产，我说如果你能扩大规模，这会改变人类历史的进程。

turns.en: Here's the thing. As much as I love the vision, I'm going to hit you with a serious objection now because I've done a lot of analysis before I even met you guys about what it would take to really scale it up.
turns.zh: 但事情是这样的。尽管我很欣赏这个愿景，我现在要给你一个严肃的质疑，因为在见到你们之前，我已经做了很多分析，研究真正扩大规模需要什么。

turns.en: It's not about the reactor technology. It's not about sodium coolant. It's about the fuel cycle. Pretty much every advanced design, including yours, requires enriched uranium fuel.
turns.zh: 问题不在于反应堆技术，不在于钠冷却剂，而在于燃料循环。几乎每一种先进设计，包括你们的，都需要浓缩铀燃料。

turns.en: Most of the advanced designs, not yours, but most of the other ones, require something called HALU, which is the high-test enriched uranium that's made from about four and a half times as much raw uranium and six times as much enrichment swoos, which is the amount of energy it takes to enrich it as compared with that four and a half percent low-enriched uranium that fuels today's light-water reactor fleet.
turns.zh: 大多数先进设计——不是你们的，但大多数其他的——需要一种叫 HALEU 的东西，也就是高浓低浓缩铀（high-assay low-enriched uranium），它需要大约4.5倍的原铀和6倍的浓缩 SWU（分离功单位，也就是浓缩所需的能量），相比之下，那种为今天的轻水反应堆机组提供燃料的4.5%低浓缩铀只需要这些。

turns.en: Yasser, I believe in you guys. I know you have a credible plan to mass-produce your reactors at scale, but here's the thing. Nobody, including you, is ever going to be able to invent a technology to mass-produce uranium mines, and they usually take a full decade to go from discovery to production.
turns.zh: Yasir，我相信你们。我知道你们有可信的计划来大规模量产你们的反应堆。但事情是这样的：没有人，包括你，能发明出一种技术来量产铀矿，而铀矿从发现到生产通常要整整10年。

turns.en: Now, right now, we don't have a problem. We've got plenty of uranium. As far as I'm concerned, dirt cheap well under $100 a pound. I think that will change, though, over the next few years.
turns.zh: 现在，目前我们没有问题。我们有充足的铀。在我看来，便宜得很，远低于每磅100美元。但我认为未来几年这会改变。

turns.en: The thing is, centrifuge enrichment plants that are used, at least in today's technology, and we're also moving to laser enrichment, but these plants are almost as expensive to build as oil refineries, and they take almost as long to build and bring online as oil refineries.
turns.zh: 事情是，至少以今天的技术，离心浓缩厂——我们也在转向激光浓缩——但这些工厂的建设成本几乎和炼油厂一样高，建设和投产的时间也几乎和炼油厂一样长。

turns.en: Every uranium expert that I've ever interviewed on this program seems to agree that there's a structural supply deficit coming in the 2030s, not for a few years, but in the 2030s.
turns.zh: 我在这个节目上采访过的每一位铀专家似乎都同意，2030年代会出现结构性供应赤字，不是几年后，而是2030年代。

turns.en: Just on the demand we have from today's reactors, before you go and start mass-producing them, we're going to have a uranium, or I should say an enriched uranium scarcity problem, especially in this halo market that's forming.
turns.zh: 光是今天反应堆的需求，在你开始量产之前，我们就会有一个铀——或者我应该说浓缩铀——短缺问题，尤其是在正在形成的 HALEU 市场。

turns.en: It's going to be really hard to solve, I think. At 1 gigawatt per year, it's no issue at all. The factory that you're building, I don't think you have any fuel problem, but I think you need to get to north of 100 gigawatts per year, and probably a lot more than that if you can really achieve what you said you can achieve in the next few years, and I don't see how you eventually get there.
turns.zh: 我认为这会很难解决。在每年1吉瓦的水平上，完全没问题。你在建的工厂，我认为你没有任何燃料问题。但我认为你需要达到每年100吉瓦以上，而且如果你真的能实现你说未来几年能实现的，可能还要多得多。我看不到你最终如何达到那里。

turns.en: You did allude to fast-spectrum reactors a little bit earlier, so I'm going to let you explain the tech, but how do we overcome this problem that if you're just running today's reactor technology, even your advanced reactor technology, I don't think it scales to building hundreds of gigawatts per year of new capacity unless somebody gets fancy and does something smarter about the way we use enriched uranium.
turns.zh: 你之前确实提到了快谱反应堆，所以我要让你解释这个技术。但我们如何克服这个问题：如果你只是运行今天的反应堆技术，即使是你的先进反应堆技术，我认为它无法扩展到每年建造数百吉瓦的新容量，除非有人想办法更聪明地使用浓缩铀。

turns.en: Can we overcome that problem? Yes, Eric, let's unpack this slowly. You're right. No fuel, no reactors. As simple as that. And so, where do we get this fuel?
turns.zh: 我们能克服那个问题吗？是的，Eric，让我们慢慢拆解。你说得对。没有燃料，就没有反应堆。就这么简单。那么，我们从哪里得到这种燃料？

turns.en: And so, I'm going to break this question into two phases. One is, what do we do today? And second is, what has to be unlocked for the future?
turns.zh: 所以我要把这个问题分成两个阶段。一是我们今天做什么，二是未来必须解锁什么。

turns.en: Right? So, today, you're absolutely correct. Most of our peers in the nuclear industry, especially the advanced reactor industry, are relying on high-essay, low-enriched uranium, so in numbers, that's basically like from 8% enrichment to 20% enrichment.
turns.zh: 对吧？所以今天，你完全正确。我们在核能行业的大多数同行，尤其是先进反应堆行业，都依赖高浓低浓缩铀（HALEU），用数字来说，基本上是从8%浓缩到20%浓缩。

turns.en: Nobody builds beyond 20% commercially, right? And what's commercially available today is really up to 5%, and then industry have been working really hard to get up to 8% lately.
turns.zh: 商业上没有人建造超过20%的，对吧？而今天商业上可用的实际上最高到5%，然后行业一直在努力达到8%。

turns.en: Now, there's a lot of investments going into production of HALU, but it will take a couple of years before this country builds enough capacity to run commercial reactors.
turns.zh: 现在有很多投资进入 HALEU 的生产，但这个国家要建立足够的产能来运行商业反应堆，还需要几年时间。

turns.en: Let's put it that way. So let's talk about today. Today, we have deliberately designed our advanced reactor to run on LEU, low-enriched uranium, that does not require HALU.
turns.zh: 就这么说吧。所以让我们谈谈今天。今天，我们刻意设计了我们的先进反应堆，让它运行在 LEU（低浓缩铀）上，不需要 HALEU。

turns.en: Okay? So, we can run our reactors between 5% to 8%, and that was done on purpose. And by the way, we are one of the few advanced reactors that can actually do that.
turns.zh: 好吗？所以我们的反应堆可以在5%到8%之间运行，这是有意为之的。而且顺便说一句，我们是少数几个真能这样做的先进反应堆之一。

turns.en: And that was on purpose because, you know, when we run, this material that we're talking about is commercially available uranium dioxide. And so, our main thesis was, hey, in the near term, when I go scale up my factory and I build hundreds of reactors, we're not waiting on a fuel supply chain.
turns.zh: 这是有意为之的，因为你知道，我们运行的这种材料是商业上可用的二氧化铀。所以我们的主要论点是：嘿，在近期，当我扩大工厂、建造数百座反应堆时，我们不用等一个还不存在的燃料供应链。

turns.en: That does not exist. We already are growing the one that exists today, and there is a lot of headroom available in not just the mining, but there's four major basically plants that's needed to get to fuel that can put in the reactor.
turns.zh: 我们已经在发展今天存在的那个，而且在不只是采矿方面，还有很多余量。基本上需要四大类工厂才能得到可以放进反应堆的燃料。

turns.en: So those four areas are mining, milling, conversion, enrichment, and then fuel fabrication. Each of these are its own industries, essentially.
turns.zh: 所以这四个领域是采矿、碾磨、转化、浓缩，然后是燃料制造。每一个本质上都是自己的行业。

turns.en: But when we talk to a lot of these companies that does mining or conversion, both in the U.S. and outside of U.S., enrichment, both in the U.S. and outside of U.S., same with fuel fabrication, turns out these companies are only making enough material to meet the current demand.
turns.zh: 但当我们跟很多做采矿或转化的公司聊时——在美国境内和境外都有——浓缩也是，美国境内外都有，燃料制造也一样。结果发现这些公司只生产足够的材料来满足当前需求。

turns.en: They're not overproducing, they're not underproducing. Most of these, they want to build capability where they can maintain to market demand.
turns.zh: 他们没有过度生产，也没有生产不足。大多数这些公司，他们想建立能维持市场需求的能力。

turns.en: And because we're not building any new plants, it's kind of very predictable how many you have to build and how many kilograms of uranium if you deliver at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 而且因为我们没有建任何新电厂，所以你要建多少、最终要交付多少公斤铀，是非常可预测的。

turns.en: Turns out if you can share the projections of our growth over the next few years, you can inspire these companies to go and scale up, right?
turns.zh: 结果发现，如果你能分享我们未来几年增长的预测，你就能激励这些公司去扩大规模，对吧？

turns.en: For example, partners on the fuel fabrication side can scale up in their current facility like about two times more than what they make today.
turns.zh: 例如，燃料制造方面的合作伙伴可以在他们现有设施里扩大到大约今天产量的两倍。

turns.en: They're not maxed out yet. So we're going to be working with our partners to scale up and build more fuel supply chain beyond what they're providing for current reactors, right?
turns.zh: 他们还没有满负荷。所以我们将与合作伙伴合作，扩大规模，建立超出他们为当前反应堆提供的燃料供应链，对吧？

turns.en: So that's the initial kind of our plan. And by the way, that gives us a moat. This is one of their strongest differentiator is we can build a mass-produced small reactor that does not require HALU and we can get to a market and supply hundreds of reactors and be able to bring our cost out, right?
turns.zh: 所以这是我们最初的计划。而且顺便说一句，这给了我们一条护城河。这是我们最强的差异化之一：我们能造一种不需要 HALEU 的量产小型反应堆，我们能进入市场、供应数百座反应堆，并把成本降下来，对吧？

turns.en: Now you're right that uranium is kind of limited if you think about mining in itself, but it's not as limited as you might think, by the way.
turns.zh: 现在你说得对，如果你只考虑采矿本身，铀是有限的。但顺便说一句，它没有你想的那么有限。

turns.en: So there are whenever and there's not a particular uranium mine. When you go dig up iron or copper or lithium, you always find uranium, uranium is very abundant in the soil, but every single mine that we're identified right now that we can tap into for uranium, we've actually just tapped into 30% of that known reserves of uranium in the mines.
turns.zh: 所以有——任何时候，没有特定的铀矿。当你去挖铁、铜或锂时，你总能找到铀。铀在土壤中非常丰富。但目前我们识别出的、可以开采的每一个矿，我们实际上只开采了已知铀储量的30%。

turns.en: There's still like two thirds that can last us like 117 more years of running nuclear power plants. Now that is if you just continue building power plants that are once through, that we're operating right now, okay?
turns.zh: 还有大约三分之二可以用，能让我们再运行117年的核电站。那还是假设你继续建造像我们现在运行的一次通过式电厂，好吗？

turns.en: You know the 5% enriched, you put into the plant, once it's done, you take it out, you only burn 5% of the fuel, the rest 95% is actually not a waste, it's reusable.
turns.zh: 你知道，5%浓缩的，你放进电厂，一旦用完，你把它取出来。你只燃烧了5%的燃料，剩下的95%实际上不是废物，是可以再利用的。

turns.en: So that material can be recycled and reused and if we do that, that number from 117 years goes up to like about 12,000 years, just from the uranium that we have currently identified, not even the ones that we have not identified.
turns.zh: 所以那种材料可以回收再利用。如果我们这样做，那个117年的数字会上升到大约12000年，仅仅是用我们目前已识别的铀，还不算我们尚未识别的。

turns.en: So it's not a matter of whether or not we want to transition to nuclear, it's a matter of when, because if you compare those same numbers with oil and gas will only last us 50 more years worldwide to run civilization.
turns.zh: 所以这不是我们想不想转向核能的问题，而是什么时候转的问题。因为如果你拿同样的数字跟石油和天然气比，石油和天然气只够我们再运行50年来维持全球文明。

turns.en: If we actually rely on nuclear that's close to 120 years and there is a little bit of a hack. If you go from thermal spectrum reactors to fast spectrum reactors, these are basically a kind of a nuclear term, but basically it's the energy that each of these neutrons have when you are in the thermal spectrum, you use less enriched fuel, but you have a higher efficiency of fission, you don't need as much enrichment, but you don't burn the fuel enough.
turns.zh: 如果我们真的依靠核能，那接近120年。而且有一个小技巧：如果你从热谱反应堆转向快谱反应堆——这些基本上是核能术语——但基本上就是每个中子携带的能量。在热谱中，你使用较低浓缩的燃料，但裂变效率较高，你不需要那么多浓缩，但你燃烧燃料不够充分。

turns.en: In a fast spectrum, you need to start with high enrichment, but then it can burn the fuel significantly more, so much so that I can get 60 to 100 times more energy from that same mined material.
turns.zh: 在快谱中，你需要从高浓缩开始，但然后它可以显著更充分地燃烧燃料，以至于我可以从同样开采的材料中获得60到100倍的能量。

turns.en: So that's what is the biggest unlock is recycling and going to a fast spectrum reactor is where you can extend it out to 12,000 years, right?
turns.zh: 所以这就是最大的解锁：回收和走向快谱反应堆，是你可以把它延伸到12000年的地方，对吧？

turns.en: That's the future product that we're going to be moving towards ultimately. That is not today, that is what we will do in the future. So the question is, why wait for the future?
turns.zh: 这就是我们最终要走向的未来产品。那不是今天，那是我们未来会做的。所以问题是：为什么要等未来？

turns.en: Why don't you do it right now? And the simple answer is, well, I need HALU to get unlocked first. When HALU gets unlocked, then we can easily switch to a fast spectrum reactor.
turns.zh: 为什么你现在不做？简单的回答是：嗯，我需要 HALEU 先被解锁。当 HALEU 被解锁时，我们就可以轻松切换到快谱反应堆。

turns.en: Now some of our peers are still working on fast spectrum reactors on day one, which I think is a mistake because we don't have the supply chain, we have to wait many, many years before supply chain catches up and cost can come down.
turns.zh: 现在我们的一些同行仍然在第一天就搞快谱反应堆，我认为这是一个错误，因为我们没有供应链，我们要等很多很多年供应链才能跟上、成本才能降下来。

turns.en: We don't have that challenge. We have a near-term pathway to bring the cost down, and then when HALU becomes unlocked and provided in large enough quantities, we have a way to switch where we're actually mining less material and we're burning the waste or the used fuel significantly more and bring the waste volume down to very, very small amount where it's sustainable.
turns.zh: 我们没有那个挑战。我们有一条近期路径来降低成本，然后当 HALEU 被解锁并以足够大的量供应时，我们有一条路径可以切换：实际上我们开采更少的材料，把废物或用过的燃料燃烧得更充分，把废物量降到非常非常小的、可持续的量。

turns.en: I made a really good point there that I want to go a little deeper on because I want to make sure everybody understands it because I sure didn't in the beginning of my exploration of this stuff.
turns.zh: 你在那里做了一个非常好的观点，我想深入一点，因为我想确保每个人都理解，因为我自己在开始探索这些东西时肯定不理解。

turns.en: My big objection in the beginning was, look, this all sounds great, but the problem we already have is the waste. There's 250,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel in storage worldwide.
turns.zh: 我一开始最大的反对意见是：看，这一切听起来很棒，但我们已经有的问题是废物。全球有25万吨乏核燃料在储存中。

turns.en: We're talking about adding to that, making even more of this horrible stuff that the public has been conditioned to believe is evil green slime that's going to seep into the water table and poison everybody.
turns.zh: 我们在谈论增加那个，制造更多这种可怕的东西，公众已经被条件反射地相信这是邪恶的绿色粘液，会渗入地下水、毒害所有人。

turns.en: What I had no idea of is the crime here is wasting that perfectly good nuclear fuel. There have been reactors designed before I was born, and I'm in my early 60s.
turns.zh: 我不知道的是，这里的罪行是浪费了那些完全好的核燃料。在我出生之前就已经有反应堆被设计出来——我60出头——

turns.en: Reactors designed before I was born that can burn all of that so-called nuclear waste and use it as fuel. So what do we do about the 250,000 metric tons of spent nuclear waste?
turns.zh: 在我出生之前设计的反应堆就能燃烧所有那些所谓的核废物，把它当燃料用。所以我们怎么处理那25万吨乏核废物？

turns.en: Stop calling it waste. Burn it as fuel and get guys like you to build the reactors that can burn and use that fuel. It happens after some recycling and reprocessing, but I just talk a little bit more about that because I want to make sure people don't come away from this thinking about, yeah, Yasser ducked the question of the waste.
turns.zh: 别再叫它废物了。把它当燃料烧，让你们这样的人去造能燃烧和使用那种燃料的反应堆。它经过一些回收和再处理后就能用。但我想再多谈一点，因为我想确保人们不会听完之后觉得“是啊，Yasir 回避了废物问题”。

turns.en: That's the big one. Yeah, you're absolutely correct. Nuclear waste is probably the biggest misconception that the general public have around nuclear, and I'll tell you why this misconception arises.
turns.zh: 这才是大问题。是的，你完全正确。核废物可能是公众对核能最大的误解，我来告诉你这个误解是怎么产生的。

turns.en: It's a very fun story that I always like to talk about. So people say like, oh, you're creating this dangerous material that's been sticking around, and in people's mind is this green goo thing because we've all grown up watching Simpsons, and Simpsons did more damage to the nuclear industry than any other anti-nuclear advocates, if you ask me.
turns.zh: 这是一个我一直喜欢讲的很有趣的故事。人们说：“哦，你在制造这种危险的、一直留着的东西。”在人们脑海中，这就是绿色的粘稠物，因为我们是看着《辛普森一家》（Simpsons）长大的。如果你问我，《辛普森一家》对核能行业造成的伤害比任何其他反核倡导者都大。

turns.en: The truth is there is no green goo, and nuclear waste is not a real waste. It's actually what we call in the industry used nuclear fuel or spent nuclear fuel.
turns.zh: 事实是，没有绿色粘稠物，核废物不是真正的废物。它实际上是我们行业中所说的“用过的核燃料”（used nuclear fuel）或“乏核燃料”（spent nuclear fuel）。

turns.en: And the reason why we don't call it a waste is because the majority of this material is recoverable and reusable and put into reactors, and you can extract way more energy.
turns.zh: 我们之所以不叫它废物，是因为这种材料的大部分是可回收、可再利用的，可以放进反应堆，你能提取出多得多的能量。

turns.en: What unlocks that? When you keep neutrons at very high energy levels, where they can go at super high speed and bombard at this material, it can really break it down and release even more energy.
turns.zh: 什么解锁了这一点？当你让中子保持在非常高的能级，它们能以超高速度轰击这种材料，就能真正把它打碎，释放出更多能量。

turns.en: And so that's number one. What is the current solution? What do we do? Where do we keep all this waste currently today? If you think about first what's happening, the waste form are metallic rods that has a ceramic inside it, and we're keeping all of these bundles in engineered casks that are just sitting there.
turns.zh: 所以这是第一点。当前的解决方案是什么？我们今天把所有这些废物放在哪里？如果你先想想发生了什么，废物的形式是金属棒，里面有陶瓷，我们把这些束棒放在工程化的贮存桶里，就放在那里。

turns.en: Not a single human or a plant was ever affected by this so-called nuclear waste ever. There's no from the commercial nuclear industry. And so it's basically a myth like it's a problem.
turns.zh: 从来没有一个人或一座电厂受到过这种所谓核废物的影响。商业核能行业从来没有。所以这基本上是个神话——它是个问题，但实际上不是真正的问题。

turns.en: It's not really a problem. We're like, well, you're making so much waste nuclear fuel, no matter what term you use. Where are they right now?
turns.zh: 我们会说：“嗯，你在制造这么多核废物/核燃料，不管你用什么词。它们现在在哪里？”

turns.en: And they probably will like spewed all over the place. That's not true. If you take all of these solid waste and not liquid waste, take all of these solid used nuclear fuel that will all fit within one football field, you know, one story tall.
turns.zh: 而且它们可能会到处都是。那不是真的。如果你把所有这些固体废物——不是液体废物——所有固体乏核燃料加起来，都能装在一个足球场里，一层楼高。

turns.en: They're not very, very big. It's very, very compact. If you think about it in contrast, the oil and gas industry, like they're working towards Hey, I want to produce energy, but all this CO2 that I'm emitting into the air as an open dump, I want to be able to capture carbon capture and sequester it so it stays in solid form so it does not go all over the environment they will live in that we breathe in that
turns.zh: 它们不是非常非常大，是非常非常紧凑的。相比之下，如果你想想石油和天然气行业，他们在努力：“嘿，我想生产能源，但我排放到空气中的所有这些 CO2 是露天倾倒的，我想能够捕获碳、封存它，让它保持固体形式，不会进入环境、不会进入我们呼吸的空气、不会进入我们取水的水源。”

turns.en: we take water from. I want to be able to sequester this carbon and concentrate in solid form so it doesn't go anywhere. Well, guess what? We do this already in nuclear.
turns.zh: 我想能够封存这种碳，浓缩成固体形式，让它不会到处跑。嗯，猜猜怎么着？我们在核能里已经这样做了。

turns.en: All of our waste form is in the solid form, very concentrated, where it does not affect any of our water streams or waste streams or plants or people.
turns.zh: 我们所有的废物形式都是固体形式，非常浓缩，不会影响任何我们的水流、废物流、植物或人。

turns.en: So which already is a great form factor to work with. And when we recycle this material, you can unlock even more bajillion amount of energy if that's an engineering term, bajillion amount of energy for humanity going forward.
turns.zh: 所以这已经是一种很好的形式来与之合作。而且当我们回收这种材料时，你能解锁更多“bajillion”（无数）的能量——如果这是个工程术语的话——为人类今后解锁 bajillion 的能量。

turns.en: So I think that's a huge potential that I think we have done. We as a nuclear industry have done a terrible job at explaining to the public what this is and what can be done with this material.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这是我们拥有的巨大潜力。我们作为核能行业，在向公众解释这是什么、这种材料能做什么方面，做得非常糟糕。

turns.en: And I think it's immense and nuclear is this very like underdog technology that we have done a terrible job at explaining to the public its true potential.
turns.zh: 我认为这是巨大的，核能是这种非常像 underdog（不被看好的）的技术，我们在向公众解释它的真正潜力方面做得很糟糕。

turns.en: So I'm really excited about the future we're forging here and the future that we can prove out to the people that no longer do we have to rely on combustion as our main source of energy.
turns.zh: 所以我对我们在这里开创的未来感到非常兴奋，以及我们可以向人们证明的未来：我们不再需要依赖燃烧作为我们的主要能源。

turns.en: Since the caveman era to now we've been doing that. Now we found out a clever way how to split atoms and release even like bajillion more energy from one atom than a single molecule of methane, which is really the exciting part about the future of energy here.
turns.zh: 从穴居人时代到现在，我们一直在这样做。现在我们找到了一种聪明的方法来分裂原子，从一个原子中释放出比一个甲烷分子多 bajillion 倍的能量，这真的是能源未来令人兴奋的部分。

turns.en: I think there's a really important public policy aspect of this, which is finally turning around in terms of sanity. But if a lot of people are skeptical listening to this, I'll come on, you can't really reprocess the nuclear waste.
turns.zh: 我认为这里有一个非常重要的公共政策层面，终于在理智方面转变了。但如果很多人听完后持怀疑态度，我会说：“得了吧，你真的不能再处理核废物。”

turns.en: The United States built a very elaborate nuclear waste reprocessing facility spent, I think a billion dollars in 1970s money, the early mid 1970s, they built the whole facility.
turns.zh: 美国建造了一个非常精密的核废物再处理设施，我记得花了10亿美元（1970年代的钱），1970年代初中期，他们建了整个设施。

turns.en: Then President Carter ordered that it be shut down and basically scrapped just as it was ready to be used. It completely went to waste because this whole issue became politicized.
turns.zh: 然后 Carter 总统下令关闭它，基本上就在它即将投入使用时把它报废了。它完全被浪费了，因为这整件事被政治化了。

turns.en: Now, if anybody's skeptical that you can really reprocess this stuff and get fuel that can go into a reactor to actually make more energy with, the story of the UK is absolutely staggering here.
turns.zh: 现在，如果有人怀疑你真的能再处理这些东西、得到能进反应堆实际产生更多能量的燃料，英国的故事绝对令人震惊。

turns.en: They did this. They reprocessed a whole bunch of their nuclear waste to the point of producing 141 tons of what's called RGPU, reactor grade plutonium, which is not weapons grade plutonium, something different, but it can be burned as nuclear fuel.
turns.zh: 他们做到了。他们再处理了一大堆核废物，生产了141吨所谓的 RGPU（reactor grade plutonium，反应堆级钚），这不是武器级钚，是不同的东西，但它可以作为核燃料燃烧。

turns.en: It can be just as effective as that HALO stuff that we don't know where to get. Why don't we use that? Well, the answer is the UK government just decided to spend, I think it's four billion pounds to geologically dispose of this incredibly valuable nuclear fuel that they spent a fortune to reprocess out of spent fuel waste.
turns.zh: 它可以和我们不知道从哪里弄来的 HALEU 一样有效。为什么我们不用它？嗯，答案是英国政府刚刚决定花——我记得是40亿英镑——来地质处置这种极其宝贵的核燃料，他们花了一大笔钱从乏燃料废物中再处理出来的。

turns.en: So they proved that you can reprocess it and get it to something that can burn in a reactor. Then they had some politics flare up and now they want to spend billions of taxpayer dollars to basically dump it at the bottom of the ocean.
turns.zh: 所以他们证明了你可以再处理它，得到能在反应堆中燃烧的东西。然后一些政治风波起来了，现在他们想花数十亿纳税人的钱基本上把它扔进海底。

turns.en: We've got to get past this somehow and I think the emergence of Chris Wright on the regulatory front in terms of US policy at least has been a massive change.
turns.zh: 我们必须想办法克服这一点。我认为 Chris Wright 在监管层面——至少就美国政策而言——的出现是一个巨大的变化。

turns.en: How are you seeing this? Because your boots on the ground actually dealing with regulators proposing to make eventually fast spectrum reactors where this stuff's all going to come into play.
turns.zh: 你怎么看？因为你的实地经验实际上是在与监管机构打交道，提议最终制造快谱反应堆，这些东西都会派上用场。

turns.en: What's your sense of how the political winds have changed? The political winds have changed quite a bit, I would say, but you're absolutely correct.
turns.zh: 你觉得政治风向变化了多少？政治风向变化了不少，我会说，但你完全正确。

turns.en: A lot of people think like, how are you going to actually achieve this? We have the technological solution baked out and proven of how to recycle this used nuclear fuel and make fresh fuel for these fast spectrum reactors.
turns.zh: 很多人会想：你们实际上要如何实现这一点？我们已经有了技术解决方案，已经烘焙出来并证明了如何回收这些用过的核燃料，为这些快谱反应堆制造新鲜燃料。

turns.en: The US has actually demonstrated this and other countries have learned this technology and are doing recycling of nuclear material. It's just a matter of a policy.
turns.zh: 美国实际上已经演示过这一点，其他国家也学会了这种技术，正在回收核材料。这只是政策问题。

turns.en: The policy is what's in limbo right now. I think the winds of politics have changed. Previous administration, even though nuclear is a bipartisan solution where both parties agree we need more nuclear for different reasons, of course.
turns.zh: 政策是目前悬而未决的。我认为政治风向已经变了。上一届政府，即使核能是一个两党解决方案，两党都同意我们需要更多核能——当然是出于不同原因。

turns.en: The left agrees that we need more nuclear because it's a carbon-free solution. It's a help to our climate change. The right likes nuclear because it's more energy security and it brings manufacturing and jobs and it creates allies who can help our allied countries.
turns.zh: 左派同意我们需要更多核能，因为它是无碳解决方案，有助于气候变化。右派喜欢核能，因为它带来更多能源安全，带来制造业和就业，并创造能帮助我们的盟国的盟友。

turns.en: Different parties rely, support nuclear for different reasons. Up until this point, whoever came in the office, in the presidential office, had never really spoken much about whether there is strong proponent of nuclear or not.
turns.zh: 不同政党出于不同原因依赖、支持核能。到目前为止，无论谁入主总统办公室，从来没有真正过多谈论他们是否是核能的强烈支持者。

turns.en: They were always shy away, especially in the recent times. However, all that I think has changed with this administration who have been extremely vocal about their support in nuclear and really put amazing people at the top of the government like Secretary Wright, who has been a very strong supporter of nuclear and making sure that we as a country are not moving away from recycling used nuclear fuel.
turns.zh: 他们总是回避，尤其是在最近。然而，我认为这一切都随着这届政府改变了，他们对核能的支持极其直言不讳，真的把出色的人放在政府高层，比如 Secretary Wright，他一直是核能的非常强的支持者，确保我们作为一个国家不会远离回收用过的核燃料。

turns.en: He's trying to bring back the notion that we as a country need to recycle used fuel and allow and enable startups to innovate and find solutions and to build industries around used fuel recycling.
turns.zh: 他试图带回这样一种观念：我们作为一个国家需要回收用过的燃料，允许并激励初创公司创新、找到解决方案，并围绕用过的燃料回收建立产业。

turns.en: You may have heard about the recent program called NLIC, which stands for Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. The idea about these campuses is that they would do from cradle to grave of nuclear and it would be hosted by a state or more than a state, like two states who would be selected, down selected.
turns.zh: 你可能听说过最近一个叫 NLIC 的项目，代表 Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus（核生命周期创新园区）。这些园区的理念是它们将做核能从摇篮到坟墓的一切，将由一个州或超过一个州——比如两个州——来主办，这些州会被选中、缩小范围。

turns.en: There's about many different states applied for it, five or six of these were down selected. They will ultimately select two states. The idea NLIC is that from developing the front end of the fuel cycle like mining, conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, to building reactors, to taking the used fuel, recycle them, make new fast reactor fuel and build other reactors to burn it.
turns.zh: 有很多不同的州申请了，其中五六个被缩小范围。他们最终会选出两个州。NLIC 的理念是：从开发燃料循环前端——采矿、转化、浓缩、燃料制造——到建造反应堆，到接收用过的燃料、回收它们、制造新的快堆燃料，并建造其他反应堆来燃烧它。

turns.en: All of that infrastructure would be hosted in within that community that can create that ecosystem that can pull, attract both public and private investments into these communities, create jobs, create innovation, ecosystem, and also at the same time demonstrate that we actually have a national solution to this used nuclear fuel problem that we have.
turns.zh: 所有这些基础设施都将容纳在那个社区内，可以创造那个生态系统，吸引公共和私人投资进入这些社区，创造就业，创造创新生态系统，同时也证明我们实际上对这个用过的核燃料问题有一个国家解决方案。

turns.en: I think that's very exciting. I'm very excited to see which two states will be down selected and we'll see a lot of jobs being created around these communities and nuclear.
turns.zh: 我认为这非常令人兴奋。我非常期待看到哪两个州会被选中，我们将看到这些社区周围创造很多就业和核能。

turns.en: If we pull this off the way this administration is thinking about, I think the future for nuclear is going to be very bright. Yes, there are some Aloe investors that I've met are crediting you guys already with being the only player in advanced nuclear that really gets it and has this mass production thing figured out and also has a strategy that eventually eliminates dependence on enriched uranium as the primary fuel.
turns.zh: 如果我们按照这届政府的想法实现这一点，我认为核能的未来将非常光明。是的，我遇到的一些 Aloe 投资人已经把你们评为先进核能领域唯一一个真正“get it”（懂行）的玩家，已经搞定了这个量产的事情，而且有一个最终消除对浓缩铀作为主要燃料依赖的战略。

turns.en: With all due respect, I couldn't disagree more. I think you do have a much better capitalized competitor that already understands every single thing that we've discussed today, just as well as you do.
turns.zh: 恕我直言，我再不同意不过了。我认为你确实有一个资本更雄厚的竞争对手，他们已经理解了我们今天讨论的每一件事，跟你们一样好。

turns.en: But I'm certain that they've already assembled a much bigger engineering team than Aloe can presently afford. And frankly, I think they've got enough money in the bank to outspend not just you, but probably your entire industry, despite the fact that your partner Matt Lozak has already raised nearly a billion dollars in order for you to build your first factory.
turns.zh: 但我确信他们已经组建了一个比 Aloe 目前能负担得起的更大的工程团队。而且坦率地说，我认为他们银行里有足够的钱，不只是超过你，可能超过你的整个行业——尽管你的合伙人 Matt Lozak 已经募集了近10亿美元来让你建造第一座工厂。

turns.en: And this competitor of which I speak has already publicly announced their plans to outspend you guys on this vision and dramatically scale up nuclear energy faster than you can.
turns.zh: 我说的这个竞争对手已经公开宣布了他们要在这个愿景上超过你们、并比你们更快地大幅扩大核能的计划。

turns.en: The competitor I speak of obviously is not another reactor company. It's the People's Republic of China. And I am deeply concerned. First of all, congratulations Chinese listeners.
turns.zh: 我说的竞争对手显然不是另一家反应堆公司，是中华人民共和国。我深感担忧。首先，恭喜中国的听众们。

turns.en: You're doing a fantastic job. My hat's off to you for your progress. But look, I was born in the United States. I have a certain loyalty to my country.
turns.zh: 你们做得非常出色。我对你们的进展脱帽致敬。但看，我出生在美国，我对我的国家有一定的忠诚。

turns.en: And I think that we have a gigantic competitive disadvantage problem forming here. This technology was invented in the United States. And if you look at what China is now doing, yes, sir, on the conventional nuclear side, they've already got more light water reactors planned or under construction than the entire US fleet.
turns.zh: 我认为我们这里正在形成一个巨大的竞争劣势问题。这项技术是在美国发明的。如果你看看中国现在在做什么，是的，在常规核能方面，他们已经规划或在建的轻水反应堆比整个美国机组还多。

turns.en: On the large scale, advanced nuclear front, they've already built and put into service what I think is the world's most advanced high-temperature gas-cooled reactor.
turns.zh: 在大型先进核能方面，他们已经建造并投运了我认为是世界上最先进的高温气冷反应堆。

turns.en: On the mass produced, what you're calling XMR front, the kind of reactors that Ollo is building, they've already signaled their intention to build an entire fleet of container ships powered by thorium-fueled molten salt reactors, another advanced technology similar to the sodium-fast reactors that you're going to be developing.
turns.zh: 在量产方面，也就是你们所说的 SMR 方面，也就是 Aloe 正在建造的那种反应堆，他们已经表示要建造一整支由钍燃料熔盐反应堆驱动的集装箱船队——另一种先进技术，类似于你们将要开发的钠快堆。

turns.en: So to my knowledge, they haven't yet announced that those thorium-molten salt reactors are going to be factory mass produced, but frankly, I don't need your nuclear PhD in order to figure out that's the obvious path.
turns.zh: 所以据我所知，他们还没有宣布那些钍熔盐反应堆将在工厂量产。但坦率地说，我不需要你的核能博士学位就能明白这是显而易见的路径。

turns.en: So my contention is that for Ollo and the entire US nuclear industry to achieve the large-scale production of advanced reactors that we need to produce in order to transition away from fossil fuels and deliver energy that is cheaper and more abundant and leads to the prosperity that existed in my early childhood.
turns.zh: 所以我的论点是：对于 Aloe 和整个美国核能行业来说，要实现我们需要的大规模先进反应堆生产，以便从化石燃料转型、提供更便宜更丰富的能源、并带来我童年早期存在的那种繁荣——

turns.en: I see the path, you're doing exactly the right thing, but I'm afraid China already intends to outspend you. So yes, sir, I apologize for the extreme length of my question and diatribe here, but obviously this is something I feel really passionate about and I think we need to talk about.
turns.zh: 我看到了路径，你们做的正是正确的事情。但我担心中国已经打算在支出上超过你们。所以是的，我为我问题的极长和这番言论道歉，但显然这是我真的很有感触的事情，我认为我们需要谈谈。

turns.en: So am I wrong to think that China's commitment to state funding, everything that Ollo intends to do and more, possesses a competitive threat, not just to your company, but to the entire industry and I think to the energy security of the United States of America.
turns.zh: 所以，我认为中国承诺国家资助 Aloe 打算做的一切甚至更多，构成了一种竞争威胁——不只是对你的公司，而是对整个行业，我认为对美利坚合众国的能源安全——我这样想错了吗？

turns.en: Am I wrong to think this and your own partner, Matt Lozak, warned Congress we can't let China dominate this industry. What do we do about this and am I right to think it's as big of a problem as I think it is?
turns.zh: 我这样想错了吗？你自己的合伙人 Matt Lozak 警告国会：我们不能让中国主导这个行业。我们该怎么办？我这样想对吗，这个问题和我想的一样大？

turns.en: So Eric, you're not wrong and it's a very interesting question. So I wouldn't pretend here and say that is not a relevant question. It is a very relevant question.
turns.zh: 所以 Eric，你没错，这是一个非常有意思的问题。所以我不会在这里假装说这不是一个相关的问题。这是一个非常相关的问题。

turns.en: China is a formidable competitor and I won't pretend otherwise. They have grown their country and manufacturing capability and innovation in so many ways that they have unfortunately outcompeted us in many different places, many different industries, whether we like it or not.
turns.zh: 中国是一个强大的竞争对手，我不会假装不是。他们在很多方面发展了他们的国家和制造能力和创新，以至于不幸的是，他们在很多不同的地方、很多不同的行业超过了我们，不管我们喜不喜欢。

turns.en: That's the truth. Okay. But let's take a look at what they're doing in nuclear, right? By the way, for the public that's listening right now, in the last 40 or so years, United States have not built much new nuclear reactors where China has been building not only existing light water reactors and have built many of these and are still building many of them right now and are getting really good at it.
turns.zh: 这是事实。好。但让我们看看他们在核能方面在做什么，对吧？顺便说一句，对于现在在听的公众来说，在过去大约40年里，美国没有建造多少新的核反应堆，而中国一直在建造——不仅是现有的轻水反应堆，已经建了很多，现在还在建很多，而且越来越擅长。

turns.en: They're also investing in a lot of different kinds of nuclear technologies. But if you look closely, you'll notice that every advanced reactor that China has put up is a technology that United States built first.
turns.zh: 他们也在投资很多不同类型的核技术。但如果你仔细看，你会注意到中国建成的每一种先进反应堆，都是美国首先建造的技术。

turns.en: Mostly as prototypes at different national laboratories, right? We built, like for example, Idaho National Laboratory, we built 52 reactors in that particular laboratory that ushered in the first atomic age and then everybody, all the other countries kind of like took that technology and started growing their nuclear industry.
turns.zh: 主要是作为不同国家实验室的原型，对吧？我们建造了——比如 Idaho National Laboratory，我们在那个特定实验室建造了52座反应堆，开启了第一个原子时代，然后所有其他国家都拿了那种技术，开始发展他们的核能行业。

turns.en: But those were essentially like one-of-a-kind systems that were essentially like started the whole nuclear submarine as well as the commercial nuclear sector.
turns.zh: 但那些本质上是独一无二的系统，基本上开启了整个核潜艇以及商业核能部门。

turns.en: China, fast forward today, they are building a lot of different advanced reactor technologies but all of these technologies is something we have built in the past.
turns.zh: 中国，快进到今天，他们正在建造很多不同的先进反应堆技术，但所有这些技术都是我们过去建造过的。

turns.en: So if you look at China as a whole, what they're doing both on the commercial industry as well as advanced reactors is they're copying off of what the United States have already done.
turns.zh: 所以如果你把中国作为一个整体来看，他们在商业行业和先进反应堆方面所做的，都是在照搬美国已经做过的。

turns.en: And that's China's model, right, is they're not very good at coming up with brand new technology. They're good at copying other innovations in other countries and be able to do it better.
turns.zh: 这就是中国的模式，对吧：他们不太擅长发明全新的技术。他们擅长照搬其他国家的创新，并且能做得更好。

turns.en: So if you think about like, well, what if they've got a lot of smart people and a lot of money in it, they can really do and innovate similar to us?
turns.zh: 所以如果你想：嗯，如果他们有很多聪明人和很多钱投入，他们真的能像我们一样创新吗？

turns.en: Well, probably, but if you look at, let's say a particular technology in China right now is a pebble-bed gas-cooled reactor. United States have been building, there's a company that's commercially developing that and China has been developing it and they got to the finish line first and turned that plant on before the United States.
turns.zh: 嗯，可能。但如果你看看中国目前的某项特定技术，是球床气冷反应堆（pebble-bed gas-cooled reactor）。美国一直在建造——有一家公司在商业化开发——中国也一直在开发，而他们先到达终点线，在美国之前把那座电厂开启了。

turns.en: It's a pebble-bed gas-cooled tricep fuel reactor, right? But you don't hear much about it and that's because they're not doing very well. You know, they're having a lot of issues in keeping that plant online, a lot of first-of-a-kind challenges and they're obviously going through those challenges and solving them, but they're not, what my point is, they're not very good at first-of-a-kind technologies.
turns.zh: 这是一座球床气冷 TRISO 燃料反应堆，对吧？但你没怎么听说它，那是因为他们做得不太好。你知道，他们在保持那座电厂在线方面有很多问题，很多首台（first-of-a-kind）挑战，他们显然在经历这些挑战并解决它们。但我的观点是，他们不太擅长首台技术。

turns.en: So that is something that we have to keep in our mind and that trend is everywhere just because China has a lot of money and a lot of people does not mean they can innovate faster than the United States.
turns.zh: 所以这是我们必须记住的，这种趋势无处不在。仅仅因为中国有很多钱和很多人，并不意味着他们能比美国创新得更快。

turns.en: Think about other industries, right? We built the iPhone, Apple built the iPhone in the United States and we, the manufacturer currently in China and the technology bled over to other parts of China and they tried to copy smartphones, right?
turns.zh: 想想其他行业，对吧？我们建造了 iPhone，Apple 在美国建造了 iPhone，而目前的制造商在中国，技术外溢到了中国的其他地区，他们试图仿制智能手机，对吧？

turns.en: And even today, Apple is still the largest market share in the entire world. Same thing in the automotive sector, Model Y is still the most sold vehicle in the world.
turns.zh: 即使到今天，Apple 仍然是全球市场份额最大的。汽车行业也一样，Model Y 仍然是世界上最畅销的车辆。

turns.en: If you think about jet engines or aeroplanes, the United States is still leading despite China having a lot more cash and a lot more people and manufacturing capability.
turns.zh: 如果你想想喷气发动机或飞机，美国仍然领先，尽管中国有更多的现金、更多的人和制造能力。

turns.en: They still are behind the United States and you know what keeps that technological superiority alive in this country is the fact that we don't become complacent on innovation.
turns.zh: 他们仍然落后于美国。你知道是什么保持了这个国家的技术优势存活吗？那就是我们在创新上不自满。

turns.en: We continue to invest in the next big thing and the next improvement, the next big innovation and be able to always stay ahead. So by the time somebody copies of it, we're inventing the next best thing.
turns.zh: 我们继续投资下一个大事件、下一个改进、下一个大创新，并始终能够保持领先。所以当别人照搬时，我们正在发明下一个最好的东西。

turns.en: And so that's something that we have to keep as a company in mind that we as a company, we have to decide, we as a country actually have to decide right now that whether or not we should let China win because they have a lot of money and people and that is a guaranteed loss today.
turns.zh: 所以这是我们作为一家公司必须记住的：我们作为一家公司必须决定，我们作为一个国家实际上必须现在决定，是否要让中国赢——因为他们有很多钱和人，这在今天是必输的。

turns.en: Or we can actually clear some of the bottlenecks in policy and regulation out of the way, put real money behind American nuclear innovation and give this country a fighting chance.
turns.zh: 或者我们实际上可以清除政策和监管中的一些瓶颈，把真金白银放在美国核能创新背后，给这个国家一个战斗的机会。

turns.en: And I think that's totally worth the shot. And we shouldn't rest on our laurels kind of saying, hey, you know, China is a big superpower. They can surpass us.
turns.zh: 我认为这完全值得一试。我们不应该满足于现状说：“嘿，你知道，中国是一个超级大国，他们可以超过我们。”

turns.en: We need to continue and pumping that American innovation and make sure we're always retaining that nuclear leadership because nuclear was invented here.
turns.zh: 我们需要继续推动那种美国创新，确保我们始终保留核能领导地位，因为核能是在这里发明的。

turns.en: We are the ones who commercialized first. We are the ones who ushered the first atomic age and we want to usher in the second atomic age as well.
turns.zh: 我们是第一个商业化的。我们是开启第一个原子时代的，我们也想开启第二个原子时代。

turns.en: Well, Yasser, I couldn't possibly agree more, especially the part about it's up to us. China is set to win if we don't take policy action to put more priority on doing the things that Chris Wright has already set out and begun doing a terrific job of.
turns.zh: 嗯，Yasir，我不能再同意更多了，尤其是关于“这取决于我们”的部分。如果我们不采取政策行动、更加优先去做 Chris Wright 已经着手并做得出色的事情，中国就要赢了。

turns.en: And I think it's so important to the future of the energy security of the country. And I'm proud to be invested in a company like yours that's making a difference.
turns.zh: 我认为这对这个国家能源安全的未来非常重要。我很自豪能投资像你这样的公司，正在做出改变。

turns.en: So before we close, please tell our listeners how to find out more about your company, Aloe Atomics. And again, listeners in the interest of full disclosure, I am a private equity investor in this company.
turns.zh: 所以在我们结束之前，请告诉我们的听众如何更多地了解你的公司 Aloe Atomics。再次，听众们，为了充分披露，我是这家公司的私募股权投资人。

turns.en: So I do have a vested interest in its future. Yasser, what's the website URL and for our institutional and accredited audience who can invest in private equity, is the series C offering still open?
turns.zh: 所以我确实在它的未来有切身利益。Yasir，网站 URL 是什么？对于我们的机构和高净值听众——他们可以投资私募股权——Series C 募股还开放吗？

turns.en: Do you have any capacity left? There's a lot of exciting things going on and we always make sure that whatever we're doing at Aloe, we're transparent and we're good at sharing that to the world.
turns.zh: 你们还有额度吗？有很多令人兴奋的事情在进行，我们始终确保在 Aloe 做的任何事情，我们都是透明的，善于与世界分享。

turns.en: So the first place, the best place to start with is actually our website, Aloe.com, A-A-L-O. We're also extremely very active on social media, LinkedIn or X, connect with us, check out our post and message us.
turns.zh: 所以第一个地方、最好的起点实际上是我们的网站 Aloe.com，A-A-L-O。我们在社交媒体上也非常活跃，LinkedIn 或 X，连接我们，看看我们的帖子，给我们发消息。

turns.en: If you're thinking about joining our team, we're seeking a lot of amazing talent from around the country to make this very important mission come to life.
turns.zh: 如果你在想加入我们的团队，我们正在从全国寻找很多出色的人才，来实现这个非常重要的使命。

turns.en: So join our team if you love problem solving and you want to solve the future of energy, this is the right place to join. And as far as fundraising, we are obviously always fundraising, we're about to close on our series C, but if you're interested, I'm going to shamelessly plug this, you know, hit us up, send us a message and we'll be happy to talk to you.
turns.zh: 所以加入我们的团队吧，如果你热爱解决问题、想解决能源的未来，这是加入的正确地方。至于筹款，我们显然一直在筹款，我们即将关闭 Series C，但如果你感兴趣——我要无耻地推销一下——嘿，联系我们，给我们发消息，我们很乐意和你谈谈。

turns.en: Listeners be sure to let us know what you think about this one. That's it for the interview time to shift to our market desk segment. Patrick, where's the trade?
turns.zh: 听众们一定要让我们知道你们对这一期的看法。访谈时间到此结束，现在转向我们的 market desk 环节。Patrick，交易在哪里？

turns.en: Thanks Eric. Now Yasser highlighted a critical requirement for nuclear buildout. Reactor production can only scale if the fuel supply chain expands alongside it.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Eric。现在 Yasir 强调了核能建设的一个关键要求：反应堆生产只有在燃料供应链同步扩张的情况下才能扩大规模。

turns.en: This brings us to centrist energy, which is the symbol L-E-U. The company supplies enriched uranium and is expanding domestic enrichment capacity for both existing reactors and advanced designs.
turns.zh: 这把我们带到 Centrus Energy，代码 L-E-U。这家公司供应浓缩铀，正在扩大国内浓缩产能，既服务于现有反应堆，也服务于先进设计。

turns.en: That creates a long term investment thesis around nuclear growth and the strategic importance of secure fuel supply, but the sector is under substantial selling pressure and we don't know how deep or prolonged this correction will be.
turns.zh: 这创造了一个围绕核能增长和确保燃料供应战略重要性的长期投资论点。但该板块正面临巨大的抛售压力，我们不知道这轮回调会有多深、持续多久。

turns.en: What interests me is the combination of lower share prices and elevated implied volatility. That allows us to collect a meaningful premium for committing to own centrist substantially below today's prices.
turns.zh: 让我感兴趣的是较低股价与高隐含波动率的结合。这让我们能够为承诺以远低于今天的价格持有 Centrus 收取可观的权利金。

turns.en: So here's the structure. With the stock around $122, I'm looking at selling the January 21st, 2028 $70 strike put. That's with 464 days remaining, so it's a leap option.
turns.zh: 所以结构是这样的。股价大约在122美元，我在看卖出2028年1月21日到期、行权价70美元的看跌期权。剩余464天，所以这是一个 LEAPS（长期期权）。

turns.en: The midpoint in this option spread is $10.25 or $1,025 in premium per standard contract. That strike is approximately 43% below the current share price.
turns.zh: 这个期权价差的中间价是10.25美元，也就是每标准合约1025美元的权利金。该行权价大约比当前股价低43%。

turns.en: So if assigned, we would be obligated to buy 100 shares of the L-E-U at $70, but considering the $10 premium we just discussed, that would give you an adjusted cost base much closer to $60 a share or roughly 50% below today's reference price.
turns.zh: 所以如果被行权，我们将有义务以70美元买入100股 L-E-U。但考虑到我们刚才讨论的10美元权利金，那会给你一个调整后的成本基础，更接近每股60美元，大约比今天的参考价低50%。

turns.en: If the option expires unexercised, we retain that entire premium. That represents a 14.6% return on the obligation of potentially owning the shares.
turns.zh: 如果期权到期未被行权，我们保留全部权利金。这代表潜在持有股票义务的14.6%回报。

turns.en: The trade-off is straightforward. Our maximum profit is the premium, so a strong recovery would leave us without the shares. Now if the sell-off continues, we may acquire the potential long-term holding at a substantially lower entry price.
turns.zh: 权衡很直接。我们的最大利润是权利金，所以强劲反弹会让我们没有股票。如果抛售继续，我们可能以一个低得多的入场价获得潜在的长期持仓。

turns.en: But that lower price is not a guarantee of value, losses remain possible, the position can always move against us before assignment and margin requirements can increase.
turns.zh: 但那个较低的价格并不保证价值。损失仍然可能，头寸在行权前总是可能对我们不利，保证金要求可能增加。

turns.en: So I would size this around your ability and willingness to fund the full share purchase. So to sum this up, we're putting on a long-term conviction.
turns.zh: 所以我会根据你为全额股票购买提供资金的能力和意愿来调整头寸大小。总结一下，我们在下一个长期信念。

turns.en: A commitment to potentially owning the centric shares is 50% cheaper than where it's currently trading today. But if the put is unexercised, we retain close to a 15% cash flow return for having sold that commitment.
turns.zh: 承诺以比今天交易价便宜50%的价格潜在持有 Centrus 股票。但如果看跌期权未被行权，我们为卖出那个承诺保留接近15%的现金流回报。

turns.en: That's a meaningful cash flow for accepting an entry price far below today's market price in a sector we believe in long-term. That's where's the trade.
turns.zh: 对于一个我们长期看好的板块，接受一个远低于今天市场价的入场价，这是有意义的现金流。这就是交易所在。

turns.en: Patrick analyzes and trades the markets every day over at Big Picture Trading. Macrovoices listeners can sign up for a free two-week trial at bigpicturetrading.com.
turns.zh: Patrick 每天都在 Big Picture Trading 分析和交易市场。MacroVoices 听众可以在 bigpicturetrading.com 注册免费两周试用。

turns.en: Now back to Patrick and Masile. All right, Patrick. We've got to talk about what happened yesterday across markets as volatility came back in many assets.
turns.zh: 现在回到 Patrick 和 Michelle。好吧，Patrick，我们得谈谈昨天市场发生了什么，波动率在很多资产中回归。

turns.en: But what's that to you the most? Well, Masile, what a day we had. It started with the opening reaction on a hot CPI and everything looked like it was the right response, which is yields higher, the dollar higher, pressure on equities.
turns.zh: 但对你来说最重要的是什么？嗯，Michelle，昨天真是不得了。一开始是对火热 CPI 的开盘反应，一切看起来都是正确的反应：收益率上升、美元上升、股票承压。
